title: Weak spectral gaps and Hilbert–Schmidt estimates
subtitle: G2 lecture 126000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: A spectral gap can mean two rather different things.
body: The spectra may be separated in one ordered direction, or every point of one spectrum may merely be a positive distance from every point of the other. This distinction also separates the hypotheses of Davis and Kahan’s Theorems six point one and six point two. Theorem six point two allows the weaker, pairwise-distance condition. The price is that its original general estimate is in the square, or Hilbert–Schmidt, norm. We will prove the underlying multiplier inequality, place it in the trial-frame geometry, and give a counterexample to a tempting stronger claim.

slides.title: Recall the two gaps
slides.lead: An ordered gap means, for example, that every point of one spectrum lies at least delta below every point of the other.
body: An interval-versus-exterior gap lets one spectrum occupy a middle interval while the other lies outside an expanded interval, with distance at least delta. A pairwise gap only asserts that each spectral value of one operator is at least delta away from each spectral value of the other. The two spectra can interlace. Their order can change as we move among eigenvalues. Every ordered gap is a pairwise gap. The converse fails. Consider one diagonal operator with eigenvalues negative one and one, and a second with eigenvalues zero and two.

slides.title: Prove the square-norm inequality in matrices
slides.lead: Let A zero and Lambda one be finite-dimensional self-adjoint operators, possibly acting on coordinate spaces of different dimensions.
body: Suppose their spectra have pairwise distance at least delta, with delta positive. Consider the Sylvester equation Lambda one X minus X A zero equals C. Choose orthonormal eigenbases of both operators. In those bases, the entry of the left side in row i and column j is the eigenvalue of Lambda one in row i minus the eigenvalue of A zero in column j, multiplied by the entry of X. Therefore the absolute value of that entry is at least delta times the absolute value of the corresponding entry of X. Square, sum over all rows and columns, and take square roots.

slides.title: Carry the argument into Hilbert space
slides.lead: The Hilbert–Schmidt operators from one Hilbert space to another form a Hilbert space of their own.
body: For self-adjoint A zero and Lambda one, the spectral theorem represents their left and right actions by multiplication in suitable spectral variables. In that representation the Sylvester map acts, schematically, as multiplication by the real scalar lambda minus mu, where lambda comes from Lambda one and mu comes from A zero. Pairwise separation says the magnitude of this multiplier is at least delta almost everywhere in the relevant product spectral measure.

slides.title: Insert the trial-space residual
slides.lead: Return to the setup of Theorem six point one.
body: We have a frame E zero, its positive lower bound epsilon, an exact complementary coordinate map F one, and the Sylvester unknown X equal to F one adjoint E zero. The residual equation gives Lambda one X minus X A zero equals F one adjoint R. We now assume only that the spectra of Lambda one and A zero have pairwise distance at least delta. If R is Hilbert–Schmidt, so is its compression F one adjoint R. The square-norm Sylvester inequality then controls X. Normalize E zero by its polar decomposition by writing the overlap as a polar factor times a positive operator, paying the factor epsilon.

slides.title: A numerical obstruction in operator norm
slides.lead: Let the first coefficient matrix be diagonal with entries one and negative one.
body: Let the second be diagonal with entries zero and two. Their pairwise spectral gap is one. Take X to have rows three, negative three, and negative three, one. Compute C as the first coefficient matrix times X minus X times the second. The result has rows three, three, and three, negative three. The matrix C has two orthogonal columns, each with length three times the square root of two. Its operator norm is therefore three square root two, around four point two four. The symmetric matrix X has eigenvalues two plus the square root of ten and two minus the square root of ten.

slides.title: What happens if the square norm is infinite?
slides.lead: On an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, some bounded operators are not Hilbert–Schmidt.
body: The identity operator is an immediate example. Its squared singular-value sum diverges. When the right-hand operator does not belong to an ideal, its extended gauge is infinite, and a gauge inequality gives no finite estimate. If the right-hand gauge is finite, the corresponding membership and norm conclusions become substantive. If R does not belong to the Hilbert–Schmidt ideal, the extended inequality has infinity on the right and is automatically true. This does not provide a finite bound. For an informative numerical estimate, R must have finite square energy.

slides.title: Do not replace the square norm by a favorite gauge
slides.lead: We can obtain other bounds under extra assumptions.
body: For example, if the relevant right-hand side has rank at most r, its Frobenius norm is at most the square root of r times its operator norm. Combining this with the square-norm Sylvester bound gives an operator-norm estimate with that rank factor. A Fourier multiplier construction gives a dimension-free operator-norm bound with the constant pi over two under general separated self-adjoint spectra. But neither argument proves the constant-one operator-norm statement. Similarly, the nuclear norm, a general Schatten norm, or an arbitrary symmetric ideal gauge requires its own suitable multiplier estimate.

slides.title: Close
slides.lead: The proof is a single idea used carefully: pairwise spectral distance controls every scalar spectral multiplier in squared energy.
body: The lower-frame bound then converts the crossed residual estimate to a directed sine estimate. Theorem six point two is precisely the place where a weaker gap works because the Hilbert–Schmidt norm has a coordinatewise quadratic structure.
